t.6.33.2: They, with horses bearing golden head-ornaments, with banners like tongues of fire, with chariots resplendent as the sun, and with charming coats of mail,
t.6.33.1: Then, as those great-souled monkeys and the demons fought on, there arose among the forces a most dreadful fury.
t.6.33.3: The tigers among rākṣasas sallied forth, making the ten directions resound: rākṣasas of terrible deeds, eager for Rāvaṇa's victory.
t.6.33.4: The mighty host of the monkeys, too, eager for victory, rushed against that army of the Rākṣasas, who could take on any form at will.
t.6.33.5: Meanwhile, as the rākṣasas and the vānaras rushed at one another, single combat broke out between them.
t.6.33.6: The rākṣasa Indrajit, of great splendour, fought with Aṅgada, the son of Vālin, just as Andhaka fought with Tryambaka.
t.6.33.7: Sampāti, ever hard to withstand in battle, closed in combat with Prajaṅgha, and the monkey Hanūmān too engaged Jambūmālin.
t.6.33.8: Vibhīṣaṇa, the rākṣasa and younger brother of Rāvaṇa, filled with exceedingly great wrath, clashed in battle with Mitraghna of fierce impetuosity.
t.6.33.9: The mighty Gaja fought together with the rākṣasa Tapana, and the greatly splendid Nīla too fought with Nikumbha.
t.6.33.10: Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, closed in combat with Praghasa, while the glorious Lakṣmaṇa met Virūpākṣa in battle.
t.6.33.11: The invincible Agniketu, the rākṣasa Raśmiketu, Suptaghna and Yajñakopa engaged Rāma in combat.
t.6.33.12: Vajramuṣṭi engaged with Mainda, and Aśaniprabha with Dvivida; thus the two foremost monkeys clashed with the two most dreadful rākṣasas.
t.6.33.13: The heroic and terrible rākṣasa Pratapana, hard to withstand in battle, fought in combat with Nala of fierce speed.
t.6.33.14: The mighty son of Dharma, renowned by the name Suṣeṇa, that great monkey fought together with Vidyunmālin.
t.6.33.15: And other fearsome monkeys, together with other rākṣasas, came together in single combat in many ways, joining battle with many foes.
t.6.33.16: There arose a very great battle, tumultuous and hair-raising, between the rākṣasas and the vānaras, heroes who longed for victory.
t.6.33.18: The enraged Indrajit struck with his mace the heroic Aṅgada, the render of enemy armies, as Śatakratu strikes with his thunderbolt.
t.6.33.17: Rivers of blood flowed, streaming forth from the bodies of the monkeys and rākṣasas, with hair for their grassy banks and bearing along heaps of corpses.
t.6.33.19: In the battle the glorious and swift monkey Aṅgada smashed his chariot, its body adorned with gold, together with its horses and its charioteer.
t.6.33.21: But the mighty Jambūmālī, standing in his chariot, enraged in battle, pierced Hanūmān in the middle of the chest with a chariot-spear.
t.6.33.20: Sampāti, struck by Prajaṅgha with three arrows, slew Prajaṅgha at the forefront of the battle with an Aśvakarṇa tree.
t.6.33.22: Hanūmān, the son of the Wind, leapt onto that chariot of his and swiftly crushed it with the flat of his hand, together with that very rākṣasa.
t.6.33.23: Gaja, his limbs pierced with sharp arrows by the quick-handed Rākṣasa, struck Tapana with a mountain peak and with his fist.
t.6.33.25: Having harassed the terrible-looking rākṣasa Virūpākṣa with a shower of arrows, Lakṣmaṇa struck him down with a single arrow.
t.6.33.24: Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, struck Praghasa, who seemed to be devouring the armies, with a saptaparṇa tree, pierced him through and killed him.
t.6.33.26: The invincible Agniketu, the rākṣasa Raśmiketu, Suptaghna and Yajñakopa pierced Rāma with their arrows.
t.6.33.27: But Rāma, enraged, cut off the heads of those four in battle with four terrible arrows resembling tongues of fire.
t.6.33.28: Vajramuṣṭi, struck down in battle by Mainda with his fist, fell to the ground together with his chariot and horses, like a city's watchtower.
t.6.33.29: Dvivida too, whose touch was like the thunderbolt and lightning, struck Aśaniprabha with a mountain peak while all the rākṣasas looked on.
t.6.33.30: Then Aśaniprabha pierced Dvivida, the lord of monkeys who fought with trees in battle, with arrows resembling thunderbolts.
t.6.33.31: Dvivida, his limbs deeply pierced by arrows and beside himself with rage, struck down Aśaniprabha with a sāla tree, together with his chariot and his horses.
t.6.33.32: In the battle, Nikumbha pierced Nīla, who shone like a heap of blue collyrium, with sharp arrows, as the sun pierces a cloud with its rays.
t.6.33.33: Then once again the quick-handed night-ranger Nikumbha pierced Nīla in battle with a hundred arrows, and he laughed aloud.
t.6.33.35: But Vidyunmālī, standing in his chariot, struck Suṣeṇa with arrows adorned with gold, and roared again and again.
t.6.33.34: With the wheel of that very one's own chariot, Nīla, like Viṣṇu in battle, cut off in the fight the head of Nikumbha and of his charioteer.
t.6.33.36: Then, seeing him standing in his chariot, Suṣeṇa, foremost of the monkeys, swiftly struck down the chariot with a huge mountain peak.
t.6.33.37: But the night-roaming Vidyunmālī, endowed with agility, swiftly leapt down from his chariot and stood upon the ground, mace in hand.
t.6.33.38: Then Suṣeṇa, the bull among monkeys, filled with rage, seized a very huge rock and rushed at the night-wanderer.
t.6.33.39: As Suṣeṇa, the best of the monkeys, came rushing at him, the night-roaming Vidyunmālī swiftly struck him on the chest with his mace.
t.6.33.40: Paying no heed to that terrible blow of the mace, the best of monkeys hurled that rock down upon his chest in the great battle.
t.6.33.41: Struck by the blow of the rock, the night-roaming demon Vidyunmālī, his heart crushed, fell lifeless to the ground.
t.6.33.42: Thus, in single combat there, those valiant night-rangers were crushed by those heroic monkeys, just as the Daityas were crushed by the dwellers of heaven.
t.6.33.44: With slain elephants in rut, as well as slain monkeys and Rākṣasas, and with shattered wheels, axles, yokes and poles lying strewn upon the ground, the battlefield became dreadful, frequented by packs of jackals.
t.6.33.43: With broad-headed arrows, swords and maces, with spears, lances and paṭṭisas, and by chariots and battle-trained horses, he was struck down and torn apart.
t.6.33.45: In that tumultuous clash, like the battle of the gods and the asuras, headless trunks of vānaras and rākṣasas rose up in every direction.
t.6.33.46: Then the night-rangers, being torn apart by the foremost of the monkeys, their limbs smeared with blood, once more swiftly resorted to fierce battle, longing for the setting of the sun.
